ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants were drawn from the Michigan Neural Distinctiveness (MiND) project, a large multi-modal study of age-related neural changes conducted at the University of Michigan (Gagnon et al., 2019).

> All participants were healthy, right-handed, native English speakers with normal hearing and normal or corrected-to-normal vision.

> Prior to enrollment, participants completed a telephone screening to ensure absence of MRI contraindications and that they did not use medications with psychotropic effects.

> All participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the University of Michigan Institutional Review Board.

> Participants completed three testing sessions on separate days: (1) a behavioral session, (2) a functional MRI (fMRI) session, and (3) a magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) session.

> During fMRI acquisition, participants completed three block-design tasks designed to elicit activity in visual, auditory, and motor cortex, respectively (Figure 1).

Ethics approval statement:

> All participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the University of Michigan Institutional Review Board.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p ≥ .180", Text = "Similarly, the within-person age effects were only significant for reliability (Figure S1D), b = -0.0091, SE = 0.0040, p = .022 (for confusability and distinctiveness, both p ≥ .180; Table S4)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

text.text: Neural dedifferentiation, characterized by reduced distinctiveness of neural representations, is a robust feature of cognitive aging.
Multivoxel pattern analyses often operationalize neural distinctiveness as the difference between within-category similarity (reliability) and between-category similarity (confusability).

However, it remains unclear whether age-related reductions in distinctiveness are driven by decreases in reliability, increases in confusability, or both, and whether these components demonstrate similar longitudinal trajectories.

Using cross-sectional and longitudinal data from the Michigan Neural Distinctiveness (MiND) study, we decomposed distinctiveness into its two components across visual, auditory, and motor cortex in more than 200 young (18-29 years) and older adults (65-94 years) and estimated cross-sectional between-person age differences and longitudinal withinperson change simultaneously in mixed-effects models.
We found that reliability was lower in older vs. younger adults cross-sectionally, and this reduction was significantly larger than the corresponding effect on confusability.
Moreover, reliability also declined longitudinally within individuals across a mean interval of four years.

These findings indicate that age-related dedifferentiation is driven primarily by declining reliability rather than increasing confusability, and that reporting distinctiveness alone can conceal substantial age-related change in its components.
Neural dedifferentiation has emerged as an important framework for understanding agerelated changes in the brain.
Broadly defined, dedifferentiation refers to reductions in the specificity or distinctiveness of neural representations (for review, see Koen et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Broadly defined, dedifferentiation refers to reductions in the specificity or distinctiveness of neural representations (for review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Koen et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: At the level of category representations, it has been commonly operationalized as an age-related reduction in neural selectivity in category-preferring cortical regions; that is, the difference in response to preferred versus non-preferred stimulus categories is attenuated in older vs. younger adults (Carp et al., 2011b; Park et al., 2004; Park et al., 2012; Simmonite and Polk, 2022; Voss et al., 2008).

text.text: This reduction in neural selectivity has been linked to age-related declines in cognitive abilities, such as fluid intelligence (Park et al., 2010), episodic memory (Abdulrahman et al., 2017; Koen et al., 2019), and working memory (Payer et al., 2006).

text.text: Although early studies focused on mean activation differences between preferred and non-preferred categories, more recent work using multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) has enabled researchers to capture the spatial pattern of activation across voxels, and it provided a more sensitive measure of how different categories are represented in cortex (Carp et al., 2011b; Norman et al., 2006; Sommer and Sander, 2022).

text.text: In this framework, dedifferentiation is indexed by reduced neural distinctiveness, and it reflects less differentiated multivoxel patterns across stimulus categories.
For example, Carp et al. (2011b) demonstrated that multivoxel representations in older adults were less distinctive across visual categories relative to young adults.

text.text: Neural distinctiveness is often operationalized as the difference between two measures: (1) within-category similarity, or how similar brain activation patterns are in response to the same category of stimuli (e.g., how similar is the activation pattern in response to different blocks of faces), and (2) between-category similarity, or how similar brain activation patterns are in response to different categories of stimuli (e.g., how similar is the activation pattern in response to faces compared to the activation pattern in response to places) (Chamberlain et al., 2021; Haxby et al., 2001; Simmonite and Polk, 2022; Williams et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Neural distinctiveness is often operationalized as the difference between two measures: (1) within-category similarity, or how similar brain activation patterns are in response to the same category of stimuli (e.g., how similar is the activation pattern in response to different blocks of faces), and (2) between-category similarity, or how similar brain activation patterns are in response to different categories of stimuli (e.g., how similar is the activation pattern in response to faces compared to the activation pattern in response to places) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chamberlain et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Haxby et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Simmonite and Polk, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Williams et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Within-category similarity is an estimate of the reliability of neural activation in response to a particular stimulus category.
If repeated presentations of the same stimulus category elicit very similar activation patterns, then those patterns are reliable and within-category similarity will be high.
Conversely, between-category similarity reflects the confusability of neural activation patterns in response to different categories.
If the activation patterns in response to two different stimulus categories (e.g., faces and places) are very similar, then those patterns are confusable and between-category similarity will be high.

Neural distinctiveness is often operationalized as the difference between these two measures: neural reliability (within-category similarity) minus neural confusability (betweencategory similarity) (Carp et al., 2011b; Simmonite and Polk, 2022; Williams et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Neural distinctiveness is often operationalized as the difference between these two measures: neural reliability (within-category similarity) minus neural confusability (betweencategory similarity) <ref type="bibr">(Carp et al., 2011b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Simmonite and Polk, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Williams et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Agerelated reductions in neural distinctiveness may therefore arise from decreased reliability, increased confusability, or a combination of both.
Indeed, some studies have reported that older adults exhibited both reduced reliability and increased confusability (e.g., Carp et al., 2011b; Simmonite and Polk, 2022).

text.text: Across studies, age-related reductions in neural distinctiveness have been most consistently associated with decreases in reliability.

Reduced reliability has been reported in the ventral visual cortex (Carp et al., 2011b; Chamberlain et al., 2021; Guerreiro et al., 2024; Koen, 2022), auditory cortex (Guerreiro et al., 2024), and motor regions (Carp et al., 2011a).
text.formatted: Reduced reliability has been reported in the ventral visual cortex <ref type="bibr">(Carp et al., 2011b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Chamberlain et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Guerreiro et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Koen, 2022)</ref>, auditory cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Guerreiro et al., 2024)</ref>, and motor regions <ref type="bibr">(Carp et al., 2011a)</ref>.

text.text: Critically, although neural dedifferentiation has been most extensively documented within these sensory and motor cortices, reduced reliability is not confined to them: it has also been reported in semantic association regions, such as the inferior parietal cortex (Margolles and Soto, 2024), as well as temporal cortex during memory tasks (Trelle et al., 2019).

text.text: Moreover, greater reliability during memory encoding predicted stronger reinstatement at retrieval and superior memory performance in older adults, including those with preserved cognitive abilities (Katsumi et al., 2021), and this finding suggests that reliability may have functional relevance.

text.text: Together, these results demonstrate that reduced reliability is a robust and general feature of neural aging.
In contrast, prior findings regarding confusability have been mixed.

Some studies reported increased confusability in older adults (Carp et al., 2011a; Carp et al., 2011b; Margolles and Soto, 2024; Simmonite and Polk, 2022), although such effects were not consistently observed across modalities.

text.text: Other studies found no reliable age differences in confusability (e.g., Chamberlain et al., 2021; Guerreiro et al., 2024).

text.text: In many cases, confusability was computed as part of the distinctiveness measure but not explicitly examined or reported.
This inconsistency raises the possibility that age-related reductions in distinctiveness may primarily reflect declines in reliability rather than increases in confusability.
However, direct tests comparing the magnitude and trajectory of these two components remain limited.

Importantly, most prior studies have relied on cross-sectional comparisons between young and older adults (e.g., Carp et al., 2011a; Carp et al., 2011b; Chamberlain et al., 2021; Simmonite and Polk, 2022).

text.text: Therefore, longitudinal approaches are critical for clarifying how reliability and confusability progress with aging and whether they demonstrate similar or distinct trajectories across modalities.

In the current study, we tested whether age-related reductions in neural distinctiveness reflect decreased reliability, increased confusability, or both, and whether these components demonstrate similar or dissociable cross-sectional and longitudinal trajectories.
To do so, we used both cross-sectional and longitudinal data from the Michigan Neural Distinctiveness (MiND) Study (Gagnon et al., 2019).

Second, we examined longitudinal trajectories to assess whether reliability and confusability change with age within individuals.

By integrating cross-sectional and longitudinal approaches, the present study aims to clarify the mechanisms underlying age-related reductions in neural distinctiveness and determine whether these effects are domaingeneral across modalities.

Participant motion was minimized using foam cushions and Velcro straps.

High-resolution anatomical images were collected using a 3D fast spoiled gradient-echo (SPGR) BRAVO sequence with the following parameters: TR = 12.2 ms, TE = 5.2 ms, TI = 500 ms, flip angle = 15°, field of view = 256 × 256 mm, and 1 mm isotropic voxels (156 axial slices).

Functional images were acquired using a single-shot gradient-echo reverse spiral sequence with the following parameters: TR = 2000 ms, TE = 30 ms, flip angle = 90°, field of view = 220 × 220 mm, and 3 mm isotropic voxels (43 axial slices, 180 volumes per run).
Each task run lasted six minutes.
>MRI Preprocessing

text.text: We preprocessed each participant's high-resolution T1-weighted anatomical image using FreeSurfer's automated cortical reconstruction pipeline.

This procedure included skull stripping, intensity normalization, Talairach transformation, white and pial surface reconstruction, and automated cortical parcellation according to the Desikan-Killiany atlas.
The resulting surfaces and parcellations served as the anatomical framework for defining modality-specific search spaces and extracting vertex-wise activation estimates.
We visually inspected all cortical reconstructions and manually corrected segmentation errors when necessary to ensure accurate surface placement and parcel boundaries.
We preprocessed all functional MRI data using a combination of SPM, FSL, and FreeSurfer's surface-based analysis stream.
Prior to statistical modeling, raw functional volumes were corrected for physiological noise arising from cardiac and respiratory cycles, using a RETROICOR-based approach.
We then performed slice-timing correction to account for temporal offsets in slice acquisition and applied rigid-body motion correction to align all volumes within each run to a reference image.
Next, we imported motion-corrected volumes into a surface-based processing stream.

Using each participant's reconstructed cortical surfaces, we projected functional data onto the individual's native cortical surface and resampled them to a common template surface (fsaverage) to enable group-level comparisons.
We spatially smoothed (5 mm full-width at halfmaximum, surface-based smoothing) the data.
All preprocessing steps were applied separately to each run.
We visually inspected anatomical reconstructions and functional alignment for quality control.
Runs with excessive motion, as defined in Section 2.1.3, or preprocessing failures were excluded prior to analysis.

Functional regions of interest (ROIs) were defined separately for each modality (visual, auditory, motor), using a two-step procedure that combined anatomical constraints with participant-specific functional activation.
First, we defined modality-specific anatomical search spaces using each participant's cortical parcellation.

Following Simmonite and Polk (2022), the visual mask combined the bilateral fusiform gyrus and parahippocampal gyrus; the auditory mask combined the bilateral superior temporal gyrus, banks of the superior temporal sulcus, transverse temporal gyrus, and supramarginal gyrus; and the motor mask combined the bilateral precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus, and supramarginal gyrus.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Simmonite and Polk (2022)</ref>, the visual mask combined the bilateral fusiform gyrus and parahippocampal gyrus; the auditory mask combined the bilateral superior temporal gyrus, banks of the superior temporal sulcus, transverse temporal gyrus, and supramarginal gyrus; and the motor mask combined the bilateral precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus, and supramarginal gyrus.

text.text: We constructed these anatomical masks separately for each hemisphere and used them as constrained search spaces for functional ROI selection.
Second, we estimated task-evoked responses using FreeSurfer's FSFAST pipeline.
For each task, we fit a general linear model (GLM) that included regressors for both experimental conditions and fixation, each convolved with a canonical hemodynamic response function.
We then computed contrasts comparing each experimental condition to fixation.
This vertex-selection procedure was carried out separately for each task, within the task's corresponding anatomical mask.
For a given task, vertices in the participant's anatomical mask were ranked according to their beta values separately for each of that task's two experimental conditions.
To ensure balanced representation of both stimulus categories, we alternated selecting vertices from the highest remaining beta values of each condition.
If a vertex selected for one condition had already been included because of high activation in the other condition, the next highest vertex was selected instead.
This procedure yielded, for each task, functional ROIs that contained the most responsive vertices while preserving equal contribution from both of that task's experimental conditions.
Using this procedure, we constructed a functional ROI containing the 2,000 most responsive vertices within the anatomical mask for each participant.

Neural reliability, confusability, and distinctiveness were quantified using a correlationbased multivoxel pattern similarity approach consistent with prior work (Cassady et al., 2020; Haxby et al., 2001; Simmonite and Polk, 2022).
text.formatted: Neural reliability, confusability, and distinctiveness were quantified using a correlationbased multivoxel pattern similarity approach consistent with prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cassady et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Haxby et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Simmonite and Polk, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For these estimates, a separate GLM was fit for each task in which each of the 12 experimental blocks was modeled with a unique regressor, yielding 12 beta estimates per vertex.

Within each functional ROI, we computed reliability (within-category similarity) by correlating activation patterns from blocks of the same experimental condition (e.g., a face block with another face block) and averaging these correlations.

We computed confusability (betweencategory similarity) by correlating activation patterns from blocks belonging to different experimental conditions (e.g., a face block with a house block) and averaging those values.
Distinctiveness was defined as their difference (reliability -confusability), such that higher values indicate activation patterns that are more distinct across the two stimulus categories.
Because all three measures are averaged pattern correlations computed on the same blocks, they share a common scale, and the distinctiveness measure decomposes exactly into its two components.
All statistical analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.5.2).

Linear mixed-effects models were fit using the lme4 package and estimated by maximum likelihood (REML = FALSE), with degrees of freedom and p-values obtained using Satterthwaite's approximation as implemented in lmerTest.
Unstandardized fixed-effect estimates (b) and standard errors are reported throughout.

Rather than fitting separate cross-sectional and longitudinal models, we fit a single mixed-effects model per outcome that simultaneously estimates between-person age differences and within-person age change (Hoffman and Stawski, 2009).

text.text: We decomposed the chronological age at each session into two components: between-person age was defined as the participant's mean age across their retained waves, centered at 65 years, and indexes cross-sectional age differences across individuals; within-person age change was defined as each session's deviation from the participant's own mean age and therefore isolates longitudinal change.

For participants who contributed a single wave, their within-person age change is zero by construction, so singlewave participants inform the between-person effect and the covariates but not the within-person slope.

text.text: A central question of the present study is whether age effects are stronger for reliability than for confusability.

To directly compare the magnitude of age-related differences in reliability and confusability, we compared the absolute values of their age coefficients from the pooled mixed-effects models described above.

Because reliability and confusability were on the same scale (i.e., from -1 to 1), we defined the magnitude contrast as Δ 𝑚𝑎𝑔 = |𝛽 𝑅𝑒𝑙𝑖𝑎𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 | -|𝛽 𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑢𝑠𝑎𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 |, such that positive values indicated a larger absolute age coefficient for reliability, and negative values indicated a larger absolute age coefficient for confusability.
We separately estimated the magnitude contrasts for the between-person age and within-person age effects.

Uncertainty in each contrast was estimated using a participant-level cluster bootstrap with 5,000 resamples, with the reliability and confusability models re-estimated within each bootstrap sample and 95% percentile confidence intervals calculated from the resulting bootstrap distribution.

The current study aimed to examine whether age-related reductions in neural distinctiveness (i.e., neural dedifferentiation) primarily reflect decreased neural reliability, increased neural confusability, or both, and whether these components show similar crosssectional and longitudinal changes.

After successfully replicating age-related declines in neural distinctiveness, we found that reliability declined significantly within individuals across a ~4year interval, whereas confusability showed no overall association with age.

Direct comparison of the absolute age coefficients further indicated that the between-person age association was larger in magnitude for reliability than for confusability, although the corresponding withinperson difference was not supported.

Thus, the cross-sectional pattern provides direct evidence that reliability contributes more strongly than confusability to age-related differences in neural distinctiveness, while the longitudinal data support a decline in reliability but do not establish that its rate of change differs from that of confusability.
Reliability, as measured here, is the similarity between activation patterns evoked by different presentations of the same stimulus category.

It asks how consistently a region reproduces the same pattern when given the same kind of input, and says nothing about how that pattern compares to the one evoked by a different category (Haxby et al., 2001; Simmonite and Polk, 2022).
text.formatted: It asks how consistently a region reproduces the same pattern when given the same kind of input, and says nothing about how that pattern compares to the one evoked by a different category <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Haxby et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Simmonite and Polk, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, an age-related decline in reliability points to representations that are less stable across repetitions, even where the separation between categories is preserved.

This interpretation aligns with computational models of cognitive aging that emphasize age-related reductions in neural gain and increases in neural noise (Li et al., 2001; Li and Lindenberger, 1999; reviewed in Koen and Rugg, 2019).
text.formatted: This interpretation aligns with computational models of cognitive aging that emphasize age-related reductions in neural gain and increases in neural noise <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Li et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Li and Lindenberger, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr">reviewed in Koen and Rugg, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These models proposed that weaker neuromodulation lowers the ratio of signal to noise in cortical circuits: neurons respond less selectively to their preferred input and more variably from one presentation to the next.
Greater trial-to-trial variability should reduce reliability directly, because reliability depends on reproducing the same pattern twice.

It does not necessarily increase confusability, though, because random variability lacks systematic direction, and confusability would increase only if noise pulled neural patterns systematically toward one another.
Consistent with these models, we found robust age-related reductions in reliability without a corresponding overall increase in confusability.
The findings also speak to whether dedifferentiation reflects broadening or attenuation (Koen and Rugg, 2019; Park et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The findings also speak to whether dedifferentiation reflects broadening or attenuation <ref type="bibr">(Koen and Rugg, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Park et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Broadening -that is, larger responses to non-preferred stimuli -should raise between-category similarity, and so appear as increased confusability.
Attenuation -that is, smaller responses to preferred stimuli -should weaken the evoked pattern relative to noise, and so appear as reduced reliability.
Reliability declined with age both crosssectionally and longitudinally, whereas confusability did not show age-related changes.
This pattern suggests that attenuation-like changes may be a more general feature of age-related dedifferentiation, whereas broadening may be more context-dependent.
Neurochemical evidence offers a possible substrate.
Age-related reductions in GABA, the cortex's principal inhibitory transmitter, have been linked to lower neural distinctiveness in sensory cortex (Chamberlain et al., 2021; Lalwani et al., 2019).

text.text: Inhibition sharpens how narrowly neurons respond to their preferred input (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011), and in human somatosensory cortex, higher GABA concentrations accompany sharper responses and better perceptual acuity, with response sharpness mediating the link between the two (Kolasinski et al., 2017).

text.text: Importantly, GABAergic signaling maintains the precision of cortical representations (Leventhal et al., 2003), and recent computational work suggests that GABAergic inhibition supports representational precision by implementing gain control mechanisms such as divisive normalization, which stabilize neural responses and preserve differences between activity patterns (Zhou and Polk, 2026).

text.text: In other words, losing inhibitory tone should therefore make stimulus-evoked responses more variable -the same endpoint the gain-and-noise models predict, reached through a specific mechanism.
Declines in inhibitory function with age have been reported in both animals and humans (Cassady et al., 2019; Leventhal et al., 2003).

text.text: Notably, this kind of change could make category representations less consistent across repetitions without necessarily making different categories more similar to one another, which closely matches the pattern we observed.
In contrast to reliability, neural confusability, operationalized as between-category similarity, did not show robust longitudinal change or exhibit consistent cross-sectional age differences.
This finding suggests that age-related reductions in neural distinctiveness do not necessarily reflect increased similarity between representations of different stimulus categories.
This result adds to a mixed literature on age-related changes in confusability.

Some studies have reported age-related increases in confusability (Carp et al., 2011a; Carp et al., 2011b; Simmonite and Polk, 2022), while others reported little or no evidence for an age difference (Chamberlain et al., 2021; Guerreiro et al., 2024).

text.text: Notably, some of these studies used overlapping datasets (e.g., Chamberlain et al., 2021; Simmonite and Polk, 2022), suggesting that differences in findings cannot be attributed solely to sample differences and may instead reflect variation in the regions examined, the stimulus categories used, or the geometry of the underlying representational space.

In this case, an age-related decline in reliability does not entail an increase in confusability.

A related pattern appears in the behavioral literature on aging and categorization, where older adults often rely more on category-level or gist-based representations and less on itemspecific detail (Bowman et al., 2022; Hess, 1982; Hess et al., 1996; Hess and Wallsten, 1987).

text.text: At a broad level, this is compatible with reduced representational fidelity without a wholesale loss of categorical organization.
However, the correspondence should not be pushed too far.

Our tasks did not involve category learning or explicit categorization judgments, and our reliability measure reflects the consistency of activation patterns across different exemplars of the same category rather than the fidelity of individual exemplar representations.
The longitudinal design complements the cross-sectional analysis by testing whether neural measures change within the same individuals over time (Rohrer and Murayama, 2023).

text.text: Reliability declined within participants across the approximately 4-year follow-up interval, consistent in direction with the negative between-person age association.

We did not formally test whether the between-and within-person age coefficients differed, and their magnitudes should not be directly compared because the between-person effect was estimated across roughly six decades of age, whereas the within-person effect is based on 58 returners followed over approximately 4 years.
The longitudinal estimate is therefore less precise, but it provides converging evidence that neural reliability decreased with age.
Consistent with this lower precision, the bootstrap confidence interval for the within-person magnitude contrast was wide and included zero (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Consistent with this lower precision, the bootstrap confidence interval for the within-person magnitude contrast was wide and included zero (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

text.text: Thus, although the point estimate favored a larger age effect on reliability, the data did not establish that the magnitude of within-person change differs between reliability and confusability.
The current study provides evidence that reductions in neural distinctiveness are driven primarily by declines in neural reliability rather than by increased neural confusability.
This finding has important theoretical implications.

Many prior studies have operationalized distinctiveness as the difference between within-and between-category similarity (e.g., Carp et al., 2011b), and they implicitly assumed that age-related change reflects both reduced reliability and increased confusability.
text.formatted: Many prior studies have operationalized distinctiveness as the difference between within-and between-category similarity (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Carp et al., 2011b)</ref>, and they implicitly assumed that age-related change reflects both reduced reliability and increased confusability.

text.text: However, by decomposing these components, we showed that the two did not change together or make equal contributions to reductions in neural distinctiveness.
Methodologically, these findings highlight the importance of decomposing difference scores that are based on multiple variables.
Treating neural distinctiveness as a single construct may obscure mechanistic differences between neural reliability and confusability.
Reliability declined both between-and within-individuals and may offer a more direct index of age-related representational change than composite distinctiveness.
There are several limitations that are worth keeping in mind.

The cross-sectional sample overlaps substantially with that of Simmonite and Polk (2022), so these analyses constitute a reanalysis and extension of a largely shared dataset rather than an independent replication.
text.formatted: The cross-sectional sample overlaps substantially with that of <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Simmonite and Polk (2022)</ref>, so these analyses constitute a reanalysis and extension of a largely shared dataset rather than an independent replication.

text.text: In addition, the age distribution is bimodal, with young adults aged 18-29 and older adults 65 and above and no participants in between, so the between-person slope is better understood as a contrast between two age groups than as a continuous function of age across adulthood.
Future research should consider recruiting participants across the lifespan and examine whether the patterns we found generalize across the adult lifespan.

Moreover, our measures were derived from block-based similarity across 12 blocks per run, which captures stability across repeated blocks rather than trial-to-trial variability, and event-related designs would support a finer-grained characterization.
Each modality contributed only two conditions, so confusability rests on a single pairwise comparison per region.

However, it remains possible that age-related increases in confusability would emerge in tasks involving more perceptually or semantically overlapping categories, where category boundaries are less sharply defined (Margolles and Soto, 2024).
text.formatted: However, it remains possible that age-related increases in confusability would emerge in tasks involving more perceptually or semantically overlapping categories, where category boundaries are less sharply defined <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Margolles and Soto, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should therefore include a broader set of stimulus categories to test whether this yields a more sensitive measure of age-related changes in between-category similarity.
Another limitation is that reduced reliability may reflect not only changes in neural representations but also age-related differences in data quality.

For example, greater residual head motion, physiological noise, or changes in neurovascular coupling in older adults could make activation patterns appear less consistent across repetitions (Power et al., 2012; Satterthwaite et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, greater residual head motion, physiological noise, or changes in neurovascular coupling in older adults could make activation patterns appear less consistent across repetitions <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Power et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Satterthwaite et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: We addressed head motion using two exclusion criteria and obtained similar results, but we could not directly account for other potential sources of measurement noise.
In addition, although our interpretation draws on theories involving neural gain and inhibitory signaling, we did not directly measure these mechanisms.

Future research can therefore integrate reliability measures with neurochemical indices such as GABA concentration to examine whether reductions in inhibitory tone contribute specifically to diminished neural reliability (e.g., Kolasinski et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Future research can therefore integrate reliability measures with neurochemical indices such as GABA concentration to examine whether reductions in inhibitory tone contribute specifically to diminished neural reliability (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Kolasinski et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Computational modeling may further help formalize how reductions in inhibitory tone degrade neural reliability without necessarily affecting neural confusability.
Extending the decomposition across ROI scales and to regions beyond sensory and motor cortex would test how general the reliability effect is.
Future research should also link reliability to behavior across perception, episodic memory, and higher-order cognition and examine how general the feature is.

Taken together, these findings suggest that age-related neural dedifferentiation may be better understood as a decline in neural reliability rather than a general collapse of categorical organization.
